lesson.title: How Big Is Big? Measuring the Size of an Effect
lesson.summary: Effect size measures the magnitude of a relationship, such as R² in regression or Cohen's d for comparing means, independent of the sample size that drove the p-value.
lesson.body:
Everything since the t-test for the slope has answered one narrow question: does the evidence rule out a population slope of exactly 0? Effect size asks a different and equally important question: how strong, or how big, is the relationship actually? This distinction matters because a p-value is driven partly by sample size, a huge sample can turn a genuinely tiny relationship into a very small p-value, while a small sample can fail to produce a small p-value even for a fairly strong relationship. Effect size is built specifically to describe magnitude, separate from how much data happened to be collected.

In regression, the standard effect-size measure is the coefficient of determination, R², already introduced earlier in the course: the proportion of the variability in y that's explained by its linear relationship with x. R² = 0 means the line explains none of the scatter in y, x is useless for predicting it; R² = 1 means the line explains all of it, every point lands exactly on the line.

Reusing the hours-studied and quiz-score data: the sum of squared residuals, SSE, was 0.8 (from the last few chapters). The total sum of squares in y, SSyy, comes from squaring and summing the deviations of each y-value from the mean of y (12.5): (−4.5)² + (−2.5)² + (−1.5)² + (1.5)² + (2.5)² + (4.5)² = 20.25 + 6.25 + 2.25 + 2.25 + 6.25 + 20.25 = 57.5. Then R² = 1 − SSE/SSyy = 1 − 0.8/57.5 = 1 − 0.0139 = 0.9861, or 98.6%. About 98.6% of the variability in quiz scores among these six students is explained by hours studied, an enormous effect size. The correlation is r = sqrt(R²) ≈ 0.993 (positive, matching the positive slope), an extremely strong linear relationship. It's worth repeating that this unusually clean number is a feature of a hand-built teaching example; real data essentially never fits this tightly.

Effect size isn't limited to R². When comparing two group means instead of describing a regression line, a common measure is Cohen's d, a standardized difference: the difference between two means divided by a standard deviation. Quick illustration: two teaching methods produce average test scores of 85 and 82, with a pooled standard deviation of 6 points; d = (85 − 82)/6 = 0.5. Jacob Cohen's widely used rough benchmarks label d around 0.2 as a small effect, 0.5 as medium, and 0.8 as large, offered as loose general-purpose guidance rather than a strict rule, since what counts as a meaningfully 'big' effect really depends on the field and the stakes involved.

The key property to carry forward: R² (or r, or d) describes the strength of a relationship in a way that doesn't automatically grow just because more data was collected, unlike a p-value. That's exactly why effect size, not the p-value, is the right tool for the next question this unit builds toward: once a relationship is statistically real, is it actually big enough to matter?
